history.heading: Island of Aphrodite
paragraphs: Cyprus, the third-largest island in the Mediterranean, has been inhabited for over 10,000 years. Rich copper deposits, from which the word copper may derive, made it an important Bronze Age centre. Mycenaean Greeks settled there, and in Greek mythology it was the birthplace of Aphrodite.
Cyprus was ruled successively by Assyrians, Egyptians, Persians, Ptolemaic Egypt and Rome. It later became part of the Byzantine Empire.

history.heading: Crusaders, Venetians and Ottomans
paragraphs: Richard the Lionheart conquered Cyprus in 1191 during the Third Crusade, and the Lusignan dynasty ruled it for nearly 300 years, building Gothic cathedrals. Venice took control in 1489, and the Ottoman Empire conquered the island in 1571, after which a Turkish population settled there.
Britain took over administration in 1878 and annexed Cyprus in 1914, making it a crown colony in 1925.

history.heading: Independence and division
paragraphs: Many Greek Cypriots sought enosis, union with Greece, and the EOKA group waged an armed campaign against British rule from 1955. Cyprus became independent in 1960 under a power-sharing constitution between Greek and Turkish Cypriots, with Britain keeping two military bases.

Intercommunal violence broke out in 1963–64, and UN peacekeepers were deployed. In 1974 a coup backed by the Greek military junta sought union with Greece; Türkiye responded by invading the north. The island has been divided ever since, with about 200,000 people displaced. In 1983 the north declared the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, recognised only by Türkiye.

history.heading: EU membership
paragraphs: A UN reunification plan was accepted by Turkish Cypriots but rejected by Greek Cypriots in a 2004 referendum. Cyprus joined the European Union in 2004, although EU law is suspended in the north. A severe banking crisis in 2013 required an international bailout.

culture.heading: Two communities
paragraphs: Greek and Turkish are the official languages. Greek Cypriots, the majority, are mainly Orthodox Christians, while Turkish Cypriots are mainly Muslim. English is widely spoken, a legacy of British rule.
The island has many UNESCO sites, including the painted Byzantine churches of the Troodos Mountains, the ancient city of Paphos and the prehistoric settlement of Choirokoitia.

culture.heading: Food and traditions
paragraphs: Cypriot cuisine includes halloumi cheese, meze (many small dishes), souvlaki, kleftiko (slow-cooked lamb) and Commandaria, one of the oldest named wines in the world. Lefkara lace is a traditional craft recognised by UNESCO.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: The Republic of Cyprus is a presidential republic in which the president is head of state and government. The House of Representatives is elected by proportional representation; the seats reserved for Turkish Cypriots have remained vacant since 1964.

The Cyprus problem dominates politics. UN-led talks on reunification as a federation have repeatedly failed, while Turkish Cypriot leaders have at times advocated a two-state solution. A UN buffer zone, the Green Line, divides the island and the capital, Nicosia. Britain retains sovereign base areas at Akrotiri and Dhekelia.

economy.heading: Services economy
paragraphs: Cyprus has a services-based economy. Tourism, shipping (it has one of the world's largest merchant fleets and ship management centres), financial and professional services and real estate are key sectors. Offshore natural gas discoveries hold future potential.
The Republic of Cyprus adopted the euro in 2008. The north, which is economically dependent on Türkiye, uses the Turkish lira and relies on tourism, universities and the public sector.
